items.title: *A*-word or *o*-word?
items.intro: Each word joins its owner with *a* or with *o*. Choose the pile it belongs in.

bins.label: *a*-words
bins.hint: mostly got, made, or taken on

bins.label: *o*-words
bins.hint: mostly given rather than set up

items.why: A head is part of the person, and parts of the body take *o*.
Clothes worn are *o*-words. You choose a kilt and put it on, which sounds like control, and the language still uses *o*.
A colour is a quality of the thing itself, a relationship that is given, so it takes *o*.
A house lived in is the place its owner belongs to, not a thing he went out and got, so it takes *o*.
Family by birth is given, not set up by the owner, so a father takes *o*.
A spoon is got and used, and things got and used are *a*-words.
A radio is bought and put to use, a relationship the owner started and controls, so it takes *a*.
A friend is one of the people taken into a life, so a friend takes *a*.
A spouse is taken on rather than given by birth, so a wife takes *a*.
The beard runs against the rule: parts of the body take *o*, and the beard takes *a*. Learn it as a fact of the word.

items.title: One thing or more than one?
items.intro: Two questions decide the form: one thing or more than one, and a particular one or any one at all.

items.why: *Laʻu* carries the specific article *le*, so the thing is one particular thing.
*Loʻu* is the *o*-word partner of *laʻu*, with the same specific article *le* inside it.
*Aʻu* carries no article at all, the silence of a particular plural: more than one, particular.
*Oʻu* is the *o*-word partner of *aʻu*, and it carries no article either.
*Ni aʻu* carries the non-specific plural *ni*: more than one, any ones.
*Ni oʻu* is the *o*-word partner of *ni aʻu*, with the same *ni* in front.
